claim: Gliosis defined as reactive changes of resident glia is the primary response of the central nervous system (CNS) to trauma.
source: Gliosis defined as reactive changes of resident glia is the primary response of the central nervous system (CNS) to trauma.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that establishes the general context of gliosis in CNS trauma response, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: In zebrafish optic tectum, stab injury drove a subset of radial glia (RG) into the cell cycle.
source: In zebrafish optic tectum, we found that stab injury drove a subset of radial glia (RG) into the cell cycle
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing PCNA+ RG after injury.

claim: Proliferative RG responding to sequential injuries of the same site were distinct but overlapping.
source: proliferative RG responding to sequential injuries of the same site were distinct but overlapping
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from sequential injury experiments with BrdU and EdU labeling shown in Figure 2.

claim: The distinct but overlapping response of proliferative RG to sequential injuries was in agreement with stochastic cell-cycle entry.
source: which was in agreement with stochastic cell-cycle entry
evidence: This is an inference based on quantitative analysis comparing predicted and experimental proportions of RG responding to both injuries.

claim: Notch/Delta lateral inhibition is involved in stochastic cell-cycle entry of injury-reactivated RG.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis and functional assays further revealed the involvement of Notch/Delta lateral inhibition in this stochastic cell-cycle entry.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data showing Notch/Delta expression patterns and functional experiments with Notch inhibitors.

claim: Proliferative RG were largely gliogenic.
source: Furthermore, the long-term clonal analysis showed that proliferative RG were largely gliogenic.
evidence: This is supported by clonal analysis data showing that most newborn cells were BLBP+ RG rather than neurons.

claim: Notch inhibition of reactive RG resulted in an increased production of neurons.
source: Notch inhibition of reactive RG, not dormant and proliferative RG, resulted in an increased production of neurons
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased EdU+/HuC/D+ neurons after Notch inhibition during 4-5 dpi.

claim: Neurons produced by Notch inhibition of reactive RG were short-lived.
source: Notch inhibition of reactive RG, not dormant and proliferative RG, resulted in an increased production of neurons, which were short-lived.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that over-produced neurons largely diminished by 25 dpi.

claim: Gliosis undergoes three significant stages in mammals: initial reactive and hypertrophic changes, re-entry into cell cycle, and gliogenesis with glial scar formation.
source: In mammals, gliosis undergoes three significant stages: Glial cells initially become reactive, hypertrophic, and inflammatory, with characteristic upregulation of GFAP and vimentin (Liddelow and Barres, 2017; Zamanian et al., 2012); subsequently, a subset of reactive glia re-enter the cell cycle and become proliferative (Gallo and Deneen, 2014); finally, proliferative glia undergo gliogenesis, the process of glial cell production, and form structures known as glial scars (Burda and Sofroniew, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the stages of gliosis in mammals.

claim: Gliosis has both protective and detrimental roles in the injured CNS.
source: Earlier studies have demonstrated both protective and detrimental roles of the gliosis in the injured CNS (Faulkner et al., 2004; Li et al., 2008; Silver and Miller, 2004; Sofroniew and Vinters, 2010; Wanner et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Blockage of initial glia reactivation worsened the injury.
source: For instance, the blockage of initial glia reactivation worsened the injury (Faulkner et al., 2004; Li et al., 2008; Wanner et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Glia scars hindered neuronal regeneration.
source: whereas glia scars hindered neuronal regeneration (Silver and Miller, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Teleost fish exhibit superior neural regeneration in response to TBI beyond embryonic development compared to mammalian CNS.
source: In contrast to the mammalian CNS, teleost fish exhibit a superior neural regeneration in response to TBI beyond embryonic development (Baumgart et al., 2012; Grandel et al., 2006; Kishimoto et al., 2012; Reimer et al., 2008; Than-Trong and Bally-Cuif, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Radial glia are the main cell source for injury-mediated regeneration in teleost fish.
source: Radial glia (RG), the primary form of macroglia in teleost fish, are the main cell source for injury-mediated regeneration (Than-Trong and Bally-Cuif, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RG of different brain regions in zebrafish can produce newborn neurons in response to injury.
source: For instance, RG of different brain regions in zebrafish, including the telencephalon, the hypothalamus, and the spinal cord can produce newborn neurons in response to the injury (Duncan et al., 2016; Goldshmit et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2016; Kizil et al., 2012; Kroehne et al., 2011; Than-Trong and Bally-Cuif, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Retinal müller glia can be reactivated by injury, giving rise to newborn retinal neurons.
source: Also, retinal müller glia (MG) can be reactivated by the injury, giving rise to newborn retinal neurons (Goldman, 2014; Gorsuch and Hyde, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Notch signaling is involved in proliferation control of injury-reactivated RG but is context-dependent.
source: As to the proliferation control, Notch signaling is involved but is somehow context-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing different roles of Notch in different contexts.

claim: In zebrafish spinal cord, glial cells have low levels of Notch activity when dormant and enter the cell cycle by increased Notch activity after injury.
source: For instance, in the zebrafish spinal cord, glial cells have low levels of Notch activity when they are in the dormant state, and enter the cell cycle by increased Notch activity after the injury (Dias et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Dormant RG of zebrafish telencephalon exhibit high Notch activity and become proliferative by a rapid decrease of Notch activity.
source: In contrast, dormant RG of zebrafish telencephalon exhibit high Notch activity and become proliferative by a rapid decrease of Notch activity (Chapouton et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Notch signaling regulates fate outputs of reactivated MG in the injured zebrafish retina, with Notch inhibition leading to gliogenesis and Notch over-activation resulting in photoreceptor cell production.
source: Notch signaling has also been reported to regulate fate outputs of reactivated MG in the injured zebrafish retina, that is, Notch inhibition leads to gliogenesis, whereas Notch over-activation results in the production of photoreceptor cells (Wan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Zebrafish optic tectum possesses a large population of RG.
source: Zebrafish optic tectum, the higher sensory integration center, possesses a large population of RG (Galant et al., 2016; Ito et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Tectal RG have been reported to be dormant and are reactivated by injury to give rise to newborn neurons via Wnt signaling as well as Notch signaling.
source: Unlike other brain regions where RG present as both dormant and proliferative forms at physiological conditions, tectal RG has been reported to be dormant, and are reactivated by injury to give rise to newborn neurons via Wnt signaling as well as Notch signaling (Shimizu et al., 2018; Ueda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: A recent study showed that tectal RG produced a significant number of glial cells (~25%) but not neurons.
source: Interestingly, a recent study showed that tectal RG produced a significant number of glial cells (~25%) but not neurons (Lindsey et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Tg(gfap:GFP), Tg(her4.1:dRFP), and the antibody against glutamine synthetase (GS) specifically labeled RG that line the tectal ventricle and extend their basal processes into the superficial neuropils.
source: Consistent with earlier studies (Galant et al., 2016; Ito et al., 2010; Jung et al., 2012), our results showed that Tg(gfap:GFP) (Bernardos and Raymond, 2006), Tg(her4.1:dRFP) (Yeo et al., 2007), and the antibody against glutamine synthetase (GS) specifically labeled RG that line the tectal ventricle and extend their basal processes into the superficial neuropils (Figure 1A–B3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations to earlier studies.

claim: Only 1.4 ± 0.2% of GFP+/GS+ RG at the bottom of the periventricular gray zone (PGZ) were PCNA+ under physiological conditions.
source: Only 1.4 ± 0.2% (n = 5, mean ± SEM) of GFP+/GS+ RG at the bottom of the periventricular gray zone (PGZ) were PCNA+ (Figure 1A–B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: One day's administration of BrdU labeled very few tectal RG under physiological conditions.
source: We noticed that 1 day's administration of BrdU labeled very few tectal RG under physiological conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Zebrafish tectal RG are largely dormant under normal physiological conditions.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that zebrafish tectal RG are largely dormant under normal physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PCNA and BrdU labeling data showing very few proliferative RG under normal conditions.

claim: Injury induces marked expression of PCNA in some RG underneath the injury site at 3 dpi.
source: At 3 dpi, immunostaining showed marked expression of PCNA in some RG underneath the injury site but not in the uninjured control hemisphere (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Injury-reactivated RG were labeled by BrdU at 3 dpi, indicating that dormant RG entered S phase after injury.
source: BrdU incorporation and staining experiments showed that injury-reactivated RG were labeled by BrdU at 3 dpi, indicating that dormant RG entered S phase after injury (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: At 8 dpi, ~69% of RG-derived clones were 2 cell clones, ~24% were 1 cell clones, and the rest were 3 cell clones.
source: In total 29 clones were collected (from 11 fish), of which ~ 69% were 2 cell clones (20/29; Figures 1M–M2, O and O1),~24% were 1 cell clones (7/29; Figures 1L–L2, O and O1), and the rest were 3 cell clones (2/29; Figure 1N–O1).
evidence: This claim is supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Dormant tectal RG are capable of proliferation after stab injury.
source: Taken together, dormant tectal RG are capable of proliferation after stab injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the clonal analysis and PCNA/BrdU labeling experiments.

claim: Stab injury can induce RG proliferation across distinct regions in the optic tectum except in the medial-dorsal region.
source: Together, our results indicate that stab injury can induce RG proliferation across distinct regions in the optic tectum except in the medial-dorsal region.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from injury experiments at different regions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under physiological conditions, weak GFP signals were present in tectal RG of Tg(1016tuba1α:GFP) fish.
source: Under physiological conditions, weak GFP signals were present in tectal RG (Figure 2A and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: At 1 dpi, robust GFP signals were observed together with the upregulation of Vimentin, a hallmark of glial reactivation.
source: At 1 dpi, robust GFP signals were already observed together with the upregulation of Vimentin, a hallmark of glial reactivation at the early stage of gliosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B1) (Liddelow and Barres, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data and a citation to published literature.

claim: The number of reactive RG peaked at 3 dpi.
source: The number of reactive RG, the ones with robust GFP signals, peaked at 3 dpi (Figure 2C,H and K)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A significant number of PCNA+ RG first occurred at 2 dpi and peaked at approximately 3–4 dpi.
source: while a significant number of PCNA+ RG first occurred at 2 dpi and peaked at approximately 3–4 dpi (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: From 4 to 7 dpi, the number of PCNA+ RG gradually dropped back to the same level observed before the injury.
source: From 4 to 7 dpi, the number of PCNA+ RG gradually dropped back to the same level observed before the injury (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 88 ± 3% of proliferative RG were located in the Proliferative Zone with a width of 76 ± 5 μm underneath the injury site.
source: the majority of proliferative RG (88 ± 3%, n = 7, mean ± SEM) were located in an area with the width of 76 ± 5 μm (n = 7, mean ± SEM) underneath of the injury site ('Proliferative Zone') (Figure 2L and M)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative spatial analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Reactive RG were primarily distributed in an area with a width of 186 ± 4 μm underneath the injury sites.
source: In coronal sections, reactive RG were primarily distributed in an area with a width of 186 ± 4 μm (n = 7, mean ± SEM) underneath of the injury sites ('Reactive Zone')
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative spatial analysis data.

claim: Only a subset of reactive RG (~25%) became proliferative after injury.
source: Although the injury reactivated all RG underneath the injury site, only a subset of them (~25%, n = 8) became proliferative (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from immunostaining experiments.

claim: The number of proliferative RG induced by the first and the second sequential injury showed no significant difference.
source: We found that although the number of proliferative RG induced by the first and the second injury showed no significant difference (the first injury: 84.4 ± 15.0 cells, n = 8; the second injury: 83 ± 9.4 cells, n = 8; mean ± SEM; p>0.05; Figure 2P)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from sequential injury experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The proportion of overlapping RG reactivated after both sequential injuries was statistically indistinguishable from the multiplication of the reactivation probabilities of either injury.
source: More importantly, the proportion of overlapping RG (those reactivated after both injuries) was statistically indistinguishable from the multiplication of the reactivation probabilities of either injury, which suggested that individual reactive RG entered the cell cycle in the stochastic manner (prediction: 7.1 ± 1.9%, n = 8; experiment: 6.8 ± 1.7%, n = 8; mean ± SEM; p>0.05; Figure 2Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis comparing predicted and experimental data.

claim: Individual reactive RG entered the cell cycle in a stochastic manner.
source: which suggested that individual reactive RG entered the cell cycle in the stochastic manner
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of sequential injury data.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis segregated 1174 tectal RG cells into five major cell clusters.
source: The remaining 1174 cells exhibited radial glial characteristics and were thus used for further analysis. They were segregated into five major cell clusters using t-SNE analysis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cluster 1 cells represent RG of dormant state (dRG) and are characterized by high expression of mfge8a.
source: Cluster 1 cells (RG of dormant state, dRG) constituted the most abundant cell population with the high expression of milk-fat globule-epidermal growth factor 8a (mfge8a, Figure 3D)
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing gene expression patterns in Figure 3.

claim: mfge8 is a phagocytosis factor that maintains the pool of radial glia-like cells by controlling cellular quiescence in mice.
source: whose analog, mfge8, is a phagocytosis factor that maintains the pool of radial glia-like cells by controlling cellular quiescence in mice (Zhou et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Cluster 2 cells represent RG of reactive state and are characterized by up-regulation of vimentin.
source: Cluster 2 cells (RG of reactive state) were characterized by their up-regulation of vimentin (vim), a hallmark of RG reactivation (Figure 3E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B1).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and immunostaining data.

claim: Proliferative RG were composed of RG of proliferative-S state (cluster 3) and proliferative-G2 state (cluster 4).
source: Proliferative RG were composed of RG of proliferative-S (mcm2 and pcna, cluster 3; Figure 3F and G) and proliferative-G2 states (cdk1 and nusap1, cluster 4; Figure 3H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing cell cycle-specific gene expression.

claim: mfge8a was abundant in dormant RG, began to decrease in reactive RG, and became rapidly diminished in proliferative RG.
source: mfge8a was abundant in dormant RG (cluster 1), began to decrease in reactive RG (cluster 2) and became rapidly diminished in proliferative RG (cluster 3 and 4) (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data showing gene expression dynamics across cell states.

claim: klf6a exhibited a peaked expression in reactive RG.
source: Kruppel-like transcription factor 6a (klf6a), the transcription factor essential for optic axon regeneration (Veldman et al., 2010; Veldman et al., 2007), exhibited a peaked expression in reactive RG (cluster 2) (Figure 3M)
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and citations to published studies.

claim: klf6a is a transcription factor essential for optic axon regeneration.
source: Kruppel-like transcription factor 6a (klf6a), the transcription factor essential for optic axon regeneration (Veldman et al., 2010; Veldman et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: insm1a highly expressed in proliferative-S and -G2 RG.
source: Insulinoma-associated 1a (insm1a), encoding a transcriptional repressor that has been reported to be necessary for MG-based retina regeneration (Forbes-Osborne et al., 2013; Ramachandran et al., 2012), highly expressed in proliferative-S and -G2 RG (cluster 3 and 4) (Figure 3N).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and citations to published studies.

claim: insm1a encodes a transcriptional repressor that has been reported to be necessary for MG-based retina regeneration.
source: Insulinoma-associated 1a (insm1a), encoding a transcriptional repressor that has been reported to be necessary for MG-based retina regeneration (Forbes-Osborne et al., 2013; Ramachandran et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: mfge8a was down-regulated in injury-induced PCNA+ proliferative RG at 3 dpi.
source: The results were consistent with our scRNA-seq data, mfge8a was down-regulated in injured-induced PCNA+ proliferative RG at 3 dpi (Figure 3O–P1)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: klf6a mRNA expression increased in the 2-dpi optic tecta.
source: whereas klf6a and insm1a mRNA expression increased in the 2-dpi (Figure 3Q–R1) and 3-dpi (Figure 3S–T1) optic tecta, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: insm1a mRNA expression increased in the 3-dpi optic tecta.
source: whereas klf6a and insm1a mRNA expression increased in the 2-dpi (Figure 3Q–R1) and 3-dpi (Figure 3S–T1) optic tecta, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The expression of her4.1 decreased during the transition from reactive to proliferative states.
source: Notably, during the transition of reactive (cluster 2) and proliferative states (cluster 3 and 4), the expression of her4.1, the targeting gene of Notch signaling (Takke et al., 1999), decreased (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data and a citation to published literature.

claim: deltaA expression increased during the transition from reactive to proliferative states.
source: whereas deltaA expression increased (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: pcna and deltaA expression were correlated, while pcna and deltaA were uncorrelated with the expression of her4.1 and her4.2.
source: Further correlation analysis showed that pcna and deltaA expression were correlated, while pcna and deltaA were uncorrelated with the expression of her4.1 and her4.2 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Proliferative RG have an increase of deltaA expression and a decrease of Notch activity.
source: Our results suggest proliferative RG with an increase of deltaA expression and a decrease of Notch activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the scRNA-seq data showing Notch/Delta expression patterns.

claim: ~82% of PCNA+ proliferative RG had no EGFP signal in Tg(Tp1:EGFP) fish, indicating low Notch activity.
source: Interestingly, the results showed ~82% (97/119 cells, n = 6 sections) of PCNA+ proliferative RG had no EGFP signal, indicating low Notch activity (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from immunostaining of Tg(Tp1:EGFP) fish shown in Figure 4.

claim: Notch activity and PCNA signal were mostly exclusive.
source: Notch activity and PCNA signal were mostly exclusive (Figure 4F1–F3).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: ~81% of PCNA+ RG expressed deltaA.
source: Consistently, in situ hybridization of deltaA followed by immunostaining of PCNA showed ~81% (60/74 cells, n = 10 sections) of PCNA+ RG expressed deltaA (Figure 4I–4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Notch/Delta lateral inhibition may be at work in regulating cell-cycle entry of reactive RG.
source: Our results suggest that Notch/Delta lateral inhibition may be at work.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Notch/Delta expression patterns observed in the data.

claim: 2 days' LY411575 treatment resulted in a ~4 folds increase in the number of proliferative RG in the injured optic tectum.
source: Notably, 2 days' LY411575 treatment resulted in a ~ 4 folds increase in the number of proliferative RG in the injured optic tectum (DMSO-treated: 24.8 ± 3.7 cells, n = 6; LY411575-treated: 109 ± 16.9 cells, n = 5; mean ± SEM; ***p<0.001; Figure 5B, C, F, G, and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Notch inhibition experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Notch inhibition was sufficient to trigger the proliferation of tectal RG even without any injury.
source: Consistent with the findings of a recent study (Ueda et al., 2018), Notch inhibition was also sufficient to trigger the proliferation of tectal RG even without any injury (DMSO-treated: 6.3 ± 0.48 cells, n = 4; LY411575-treated: 26.7 ± 2.4 cells, n = 5; mean ± SEM; p>0.05; Figure 5D, E, H, I, J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Notch inhibition experiments and a citation to a published study.

claim: ~94% of NICD-overexpressed RG underneath the injury sites were PCNA−.
source: Mis-expression of NICD significantly blocked the cell-cycle entry of tectal RG following stab injury, that is, ~94% (31/33 cells, n = 15 sections) of NICD-overexpressed RG underneath the injury sites were PCNA− (Figure 5L–N and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-E3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from NICD overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Notch inhibition mediates the stochastic cell-cycle entry of reactive RG after the injury.
source: In sum, Notch inhibition mediates the stochastic cell-cycle entry of reactive RG after the injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Notch inhibition and overexpression experiments.

claim: The newborn cells from proliferative RG were largely BLBP positive, indicative of RG identity.
source: Notably, the newborn cells were largely BLBP positive, indicative of RG identity (Figure 6A–B3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6.

claim: EdU+ newborn cells were largely EdU+/BLBP+ RG (90.5 ± 1.4% of total EdU+ cells) rather than EdU+/HuC/D+ newborn neurons (3.3 ± 0.9% of total EdU+ cells) in the injured hemisphere at 7 dpi.
source: Notably, EdU+ newborn cells were largely EdU+/BLBP+ RG (78.6 ± 5.9 cells, 90.5 ± 1.4% of total EdU+ cells, n = 8, mean ± SEM) rather than EdU+/HuC/D+ newborn neurons (3 ± 1.0 cells, 3.3 ± 0.9% of total EdU+ cells, n = 7, mean ± SEM) in the injured hemisphere, indicating that tectal RG largely undergo gliogenesis (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from EdU pulse-and-stain assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: Tectal RG largely undergo gliogenesis after injury.
source: indicating that tectal RG largely undergo gliogenesis
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EdU labeling data showing predominantly glial cell production.

claim: Glial bulges formed underneath the injury sites as a consequence of gliogenesis.
source: As a consequence, glial bulges formed underneath the injury sites (Figure 6D–E3).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: At ~300 dpi, the glial bulges remained and were still largely composed of EdU+/BLBP+ RG (93.6 ± 0.7% of total EdU+ cells).
source: More importantly, when we analyzed EdU+ newborn cells at ~300 dpi (Figure 6I), the glial bulges remained and were still largely composed of EdU+/BLBP+ RG (111.3 ± 9.4 cells, 93.6 ± 0.7% of total EdU+ cells, n = 3, mean ± SEM; Figure 6J–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by long-term tracing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Only a few EdU+ cells were EdU+/HuC/D+ neurons (1.6 ± 0.4% of total EdU+ cells) at ~300 dpi.
source: Only a few EdU+ cells were EdU+/HuC/D+ neurons (2 ± 0.6 cells, 1.6 ± 0.4% of total EdU+ cells, n = 3; mean ± SEM, Figure 6J–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by long-term tracing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Stab injury triggers the gliogenesis of tectal RG, resulting in the formation of glial bulges in the zebrafish optic tectum.
source: Together, stab injury triggers the gliogenesis of tectal RG, resulting in the formation of glial bulges in the zebrafish optic tectum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EdU labeling and long-term tracing data.

claim: Stab wounds remained up to 300–400 dpi.
source: More strikingly, these stab wounds remained up to 300–400 dpi (1339 ± 768.6 μm2, n = 7, mean ± SEM; p>0.05; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F-I3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from long-term analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hypertrophic processes of RG formed a glial scar-like structure surrounding the wound, thereby blocking the repair of the wound.
source: These wounds were surrounded by BLBP signals but without cell nuclei, suggesting that the hypertrophic processes of RG formed a glial scar-like structure surrounding the wound, and thereby blocking the repair of the wound (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B3 and F-I3).
evidence: This is an inference based on imaging data showing BLBP+ processes surrounding wounds.

claim: The results suggest a limited regenerative capacity of the adult zebrafish optic tectum.
source: Our results suggest a limited regenerative capacity of the adult zebrafish optic tectum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of persistent wounds and glial scar formation.

claim: Notch inhibition during 4–5 dpi but not 1–3 dpi results in a significant increase in newborn neurons.
source: Indeed, we find that post-injury Notch inhibition during 4–5 dpi but not 1–3 dpi results in a significant increase in newborn neurons (Figure 7A–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Notch inhibition experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Notch inhibition (4–5 dpi) of injury-induced reactive RG labeled during 4–6 dpi results in a significant increase of neuron production.
source: Our further analysis shows that Notch inhibition (4–5 dpi) of injury-induced reactive RG labeled during 4–6 dpi results in a significant increase of neuron production (Figure 7I, L, M, O and P).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from EdU labeling experiments with Notch inhibition shown in Figure 7.

claim: No significant change of neuron production from injury-induced proliferative RG labeled during 1–3 dpi is observed with Notch inhibition.
source: No significant change of neuron production from injury-induced proliferative RG labeled during 1–3 dpi is observed (Figure 7H, J, K, O and P).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cell states of tectal RG, such as dormant state, reactive state, or proliferative state, influence their fate outcomes in the context of Notch inhibition or injury.
source: Our findings raised an interesting hypothesis, that is, cell states of tectal RG, such as dormant state, reactive state, or proliferative state, influence their fate outcomes in the context of Notch inhibition or injury (Figure 7Q).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the differential responses of RG in different states to Notch inhibition.

claim: Over-produced neurons disappeared by 25 dpi.
source: Besides, long-term experiments unexpectedly showed that over-produced neurons disappeared by 25 dpi.
evidence: This claim is supported by long-term tracing data showing a decrease in neuron numbers.

claim: The number of newborn neurons in LY411575-treated fish decreased significantly at 25 dpi compared to 7 dpi.
source: Interestingly, the number of newborn neurons in LY411575-treated fish decreased significantly at 25 dpi (EdU+/HuC/D+; 7-dpi LY411575-treated: 15.9 ± 2.7 cells, n = 10; 25-dpi LY411575-treated: 2.4 ± 0.3 cells, n = 14; mean ± SEM; ***p<0.001) and became indistinguishable from the DMSO-treated fish (p>0.05; Figure 7—figure supplement 1I, K and N).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from long-term tracing experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The remaining newborn neurons could survive until ~86 dpi.
source: The remaining newborn neurons could survive until ~86 dpi (Figure 7—figure supplement 1O–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by long-term tracing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: 76% of long-lived neurons resided in the tectum opticum (TeO) in 25-dpi LY411575-treated fish.
source: 76% of long-lived neurons resided in the tectum opticum (TeO) in 25-dpi LY411575-treated fish (25 dpi DMSO-treated: 83%; Figure 7—figure supplement 1Q–S).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Post-injury Notch inhibition did not help to complete restoration of the injured optic tectum.
source: We measured the wound area (1669 ± 704.3 μm2, n = 3, mean ± SEM) and found that the post-injury Notch inhibition did not help to complete restoration of the injured optic tectum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1T and U).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data measuring wound area shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zebrafish tectal RG are undergoing the consecutive phases of glial reactivation and glial proliferation in response to injury, consistent with astrogliosis in injured mammalian CNS.
source: Consistent with astrogliosis in injured mammalian CNS, we find that zebrafish tectal RG are undergoing the consecutive phases of glial reactivation and glial proliferation in response to the injury (Figure 2A–K) (Burda and Sofroniew, 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal analysis of RG responses and a citation to published literature.

claim: After stab injury, almost all RG underneath the injury site respond to the injury by glial reactivation, characterized with the up-regulation of vimentin expression and robust GFP expression in Tg(1016tuba1α:GFP).
source: After stab injury, almost all RG underneath the injury site respond to the injury by glial reactivation, characterized with the up-regulation of vimentin expression and robust GFP expression in a powerful transgenic line Tg(1016tuba1α:GFP), which has been used to monitor the injury-induced MG in zebrafish retina (Fausett and Goldman, 2006; Wan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data and citations to published studies.

claim: After reactivation, ~25% of RG are entering the cell cycle and become proliferative.
source: After the reactivation, ~25% of RG are entering the cell cycle, and become proliferative (Figure 2H, L and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I-J2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from immunostaining experiments.

claim: The proliferative RG that respond to two sequential injuries are distinct but overlapping, which can be well explained by stochastic cell-cycle entry.
source: More interestingly, we find that the proliferative RG that respond to two sequential injuries are distinct but overlapping, which can be well explained by stochastic cell-cycle entry.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequential injury experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: Tectal RG underneath the injury sites randomly enter the cell cycle.
source: It is, unexpectedly, that tectal RG underneath the injury sites randomly enter the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stochastic analysis of cell-cycle entry.

claim: Proliferative RG have high deltaA expression while non-proliferating RG have high Notch activity, pointing to the working of Notch/Delta lateral inhibition.
source: Our results show that proliferative RG have high deltaA expression while non-proliferating RG have high Notch activity, pointing to the working of Notch/Delta lateral inhibition, reminiscent of the function of Notch/Delta lateral inhibition in stochastically determining the fate of neuroblasts in Drosophila (Sato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scRNA-seq and immunostaining data, with a citation to a published study.

claim: Notch/Delta lateral inhibition functions in stochastically determining the fate of neuroblasts in Drosophila.
source: reminiscent of the function of Notch/Delta lateral inhibition in stochastically determining the fate of neuroblasts in Drosophila (Sato et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Using EdU pulse-and-stain assay and Cre-loxP-based clonal analysis of tectal RG, we unambiguously demonstrate at the single-cell resolution that RG give rise to newborn glial cells (~91% of total newborn cells) with only a few neurons (~3–5% of total newborn cells) after the injury.
source: Using EdU pulse-and-stain assay and Cre-loxP-based clonal analysis of tectal RG, we unambiguously demonstrate at the single-cell resolution that RG give rise to newborn glial cells (~91% of total newborn cells) with only a few neurons (~3–5% of total newborn cells) after the injury (Figure 7Q)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from EdU labeling and clonal analysis experiments.

claim: The average number of newborn neurons in the study from Ohshima's lab (~4 BrdU+/HuC/D+ neurons) was mostly similar to what we had (~4 EdU+/HuC/D+ neurons).
source: In fact, the average number of newborn neurons in the study from Ohshima's lab (~4 BrdU+/HuC/D+ neurons) was mostly similar to what we had (~4 EdU+/HuC/D+ neurons)
evidence: This is a comparison with published data to reconcile differences in conclusions.

claim: The number of total newborn cells in Ohshima's study (~17 BrdU+ cells) is much smaller than ours (~90 EdU+ cells).
source: while the number of total newborn cells in their study (~17 BrdU+ cells) is much smaller than ours (~90 EdU+ cells)
evidence: This is a comparison with published data to explain differences in conclusions.

claim: The conclusion of a high proportion of newborn neurons from Ohshima's lab is perhaps due to the underestimated number of total newborn cells.
source: Thus, the conclusion of a high proportion of newborn neurons from Ohshima's lab is perhaps due to the underestimated number of total newborn cells.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the discrepancy with published data.

claim: hmgb2a and hmgb2b are highly expressed in RG of proliferative state.
source: Our scRNA-seq data shows that hmgb2a and hmgb2b are highly expressed in RG of proliferative state (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: hmgb2 is strongly associated with dormancy/activation transition of adult neural stem cells (NSCs) in mice.
source: hmgb2 is strongly associated with dormancy/activation transition of adult neural stem cells (NSCs) in mice (Kimura et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Loss of hmgb2 compromises gliogenesis and promotes neurogenesis.
source: and loss of hmgb2 compromises gliogenesis and promotes neurogenesis (Abraham et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In situ hybridization confirms the expression of hmgb2a in the proliferating tectal RG as the result of stab injury.
source: In situ hybridization also confirm the expression of hmgb2a in the proliferating tectal RG as the result of stab injury (Figure 6—figure supplement 1L-M2)
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Proliferative tectal RG are likely to be gliogenic.
source: suggesting proliferative tectal RG are likely to be gliogenic
evidence: This is an inference based on hmgb2a expression data and published literature on hmgb2 function.

claim: Tectal RG resembles mammalian astrocytes in terms of injury response, undergoing gliogenesis rather than neurogenesis.
source: Thus, unlike to RG of other CNS regions in zebrafish (Dias et al., 2012; Goldman, 2014; Kizil et al., 2012; Kroehne et al., 2011; Than-Trong and Bally-Cuif, 2015), tectal RG resembles mammalian astrocytes in terms of injury response, undergoing the gliogenesis rather than the neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fate analysis data and comparison with published literature.

claim: Newborn glial cells are unable to migrate to the injury sites and the wounds are not restored.
source: which suggests that newborn glial cells are unable to migrate to the injury sites and the wounds are not restored
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of persistent wounds and glial bulge formation.

claim: Down-regulation of Notch signaling is profoundly implicated in the production of neurons during embryonic CNS development.
source: Down-regulation of Notch signaling is profoundly implicated in the production of neurons during embryonic CNS development (Beatus and Lendahl, 1998; Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Notch inhibition itself did not promote the neurogenesis of injury-induced proliferative RG.
source: which suggested that Notch inhibition itself did not promote the neurogenesis of injury-induced proliferative RG (Figure 7P)
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EdU labeling experiments with Notch inhibition.

claim: Post-injury Notch inhibition (4–5 dpi) drives injury-induced reactive RG (non-proliferation) into the cell cycle, producing a significantly higher proportion of neurons compared to those derived from proliferative RG by either the injury or Notch inhibition.
source: Together, our results suggest that post-injury Notch inhibition (4–5 dpi) drives injury-induced reactive RG (non-proliferation) into the cell cycle, producing a significantly higher proportion of neurons compared to those derived from proliferative RG by either the injury (5.3 ± 1.1%, n = 6, mean ± SEM) or Notch inhibition (1.2 ± 0.6%, n = 7, mean ± SEM) (Figure 7G and Q).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative analysis of EdU labeling experiments with different Notch inhibition timings.

claim: The rapid loss of over-produced neurons might be due to their intrinsic property of short life or due to the lack of significant neuron loss in stab injured optic tectum.
source: Our observation of rapid loss of newborn cells might be due to their intrinsic property of short life or due to the lack of significant neuron loss in stab injured optic tectum.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanisms underlying the loss of over-produced neurons.
